direction_summaries.explanation: It appears this feature is picking up on an end‐of–lexical unit or “boundary” signal—especially in formal, structured text (think addresses, document headers, dates, titles, and abbreviations) where a punctuation mark (typically a period) correctly ends a token. With the feature present the model “knows” to finish the unit (yielding a period and then a number, name or proper continuation), while without it the continuation instead runs into sub‐word fragments (e.g. “mn”, “vention”, “million”) that don’t fit. In short, it represents a learned cue for punctuation/abbreviation boundaries in structured text that helps guide proper next‐token generation.

direction_summaries.explanation: It appears that this feature “lights up” on the beginning fragments of proper‐noun tokens (often names, places, or branded entities) that are split from their “continuation” suffix. In other words, it signals that the current token is only a prefix (for example “Den” in “Denver”, “Denise” or “Tenterden”, “Fel” in “Felicia”, “Fed” in “Fedora”, “Ama” in “Amazing”, etc.) so that the model will complete the compound name appropriately. Removing the feature makes the model lose that context and default to a generic continuation (“themselves”), confirming its role in bundling together these split subwords into the intended proper name or term.

direction_summaries.explanation: It appears that this feature encodes a signal about word‐ or morpheme‐boundaries. In other words, it tells the model “this token is complete” (or should be treated as an independent word) rather than an unfinished stem needing an extra affix (like “s,” “ly,” or “uality”). This boundary signal shifts the next–token prediction from one that would continue a word to one that appropriately begins a new word or punctuation, reflecting an internal awareness of morphological segmentation.

direction_summaries.explanation: It appears that this feature “lights up” on the beginning fragments of proper‐noun tokens (often names, places, or branded entities) that are split from their “continuation” suffix. In other words, it signals that the current token is only a prefix (for example “Den” in “Denver”, “Denise” or “Tenterden”, “Fel” in “Felicia”, “Fed” in “Fedora”, “Ama” in “Amazing”, etc.) so that the model will complete the compound name appropriately. Removing the feature makes the model lose that context and default to a generic continuation (“themselves”), confirming its role in bundling together these split subwords into the intended proper name or term.

direction_summaries.explanation: It’s a “sentence‐boundary” signal—the model’s internal marker for a terminal period that switches the context from one sentence to a new one. With the feature present the model “knows” to finish the unit (yielding a period and then a number, name or proper continuation), while without it the continuation instead runs into sub‐word fragments (e.g. “mn”, “vention”, “million”) that don’t fit. In short, it represents a learned cue for punctuation/abbreviation boundaries in structured text that helps guide proper next‐token generation.

In short, this feature signals a morphologically or orthographically “incomplete” unit whose tail cues the model to merge with a following piece, so that when it’s removed the next token’s prediction (often “P” or another letter starting the proper continuation) shifts.

direction_summaries.explanation: It appears this feature is picking up on an end‐of–lexical unit or “boundary” signal—especially in formal, structured text (think addresses, document headers, dates, titles, and abbreviations) where a punctuation mark (typically a period) correctly ends a token. With the feature present the model “knows” to finish the unit (yielding a period and then a number, name or proper continuation), while without it the continuation instead runs into sub‐word fragments (e.g. “mn”, “vention”, “million”) that don’t fit. In short, it represents a learned cue for punctuation/abbreviation boundaries in structured text that helps guide proper next‐token generation.

direction_summaries.explanation: It appears that this feature “lights up” on the beginning fragments of proper‐noun tokens (often names, places, or branded entities) that are split from their “continuation” suffix. In other words, it signals that the current token is only a prefix (for example “Den” in “Denver”, “Denise” or “Tenterden”, “Fel” in “Felicia”, “Fed” in “Fedora”, “Ama” in “Amazing”, etc.) so that the model will complete the compound name appropriately. Removing the feature makes the model lose that context and default to a generic continuation (“themselves”), confirming its role in bundling together these split subwords into the intended proper name or term.

direction_summaries.explanation: It’s a “sentence‐boundary” signal—the model’s internal marker for a terminal period that switches the context from one sentence to a new one. direction_summaries.explanation: It appears that the model has learned a “subword‐continuation” signal—that is, a detector for particular word‐ending (or “affix”) fragments (as in “ino,” “amb,” “lif,” “ov,” “pt,” etc.) that mark that the token is only a part of a larger word. In short, this feature signals a morphologically or orthographically “incomplete” unit whose tail cues the model to merge with a following piece, so that when it’s removed the next token’s prediction (often “P” or another letter starting the proper continuation) shifts.

direction_summaries.explanation: It appears to be a “sentence‐or sentence‐segment initiation” feature—that is, a signal that a new, often stylized or headline‐like statement is beginning. This feature activates on the very first (or initial fragment) token of a sentence or announcement and helps set up the expected syntactic and stylistic continuation (for example, an imperative or promotional tone), so that when it’s present the model predicts the conventional next functor (like “to” or a punctuation), whereas without it the following word form can shift slightly.
